title: Regression metrics: MSE, RMSE, MAE & R²
intro: Four standard regression measures — MSE, RMSE, MAE and R² — with formulas, a worked car-price example, the exact formulas for b1 and b0, and interactive plots with live metrics.
keyPoints: MSE = mean squared error; RMSE = its square root, in y's own units.
MAE is robust to outliers; MSE/RMSE punish large mistakes extra hard.
R² = explained variance: 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than predicting the mean.
The best-fit line analytically: b1 = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)² and b0 = ȳ − b1·x̄.

blocks.html: In regression everything revolves around one question: how far are the predictions \( \hat{y} \) from the true values \( y \)? Note the distinction: the loss is for training (mathematically convenient), the metric for judging (human-readable).

rows: after fit(), on the test set

blocks.html: You evaluate every metric below on the test set, not on the training set. On training data the numbers can look great while the model has simply memorised the data (overfitting) — see the ML workflow.

sections.title: The three error measures: MSE, RMSE and MAE

blocks.html: The three most used measures — MSE, RMSE and MAE — all capture the average deviation, each in its own way; you feel the difference mostly with outliers.

blocks.label: Mean Squared Error
blocks.caption: Squares every error and averages: large errors count extra heavily.

blocks.label: Root Mean Squared Error
blocks.caption: The square root of the MSE — back in the same unit as the target, which makes interpretation easier.

blocks.label: Mean Absolute Error
blocks.caption: Takes the absolute error: more robust against outliers, but harder to differentiate.

blocks.html: Symbols: \( N \) = number of points, \( y_i \) = true value, \( \hat{y}_i \) = prediction; the difference \( y_i - \hat{y}_i \) is one prediction's error (the residual).
MSE vs MAE with outliers: an error of 10 becomes \( 10^2 = 100 \) under MSE but just 10 under MAE — one extreme error dominates the MSE, while MAE only grows linearly.

sections.title: Example: predicting the price of a car

blocks.html: Linear regression with three features on five cars. After training: \( b_0 = 20 \), \( b_1 = -1 \), \( b_2 = -0.5 \), \( b_3 = -2 \). The prediction equation:

blocks.label: car price prediction
blocks.caption: Substitute each car's feature values into the formula and you get its predicted price.

blocks.html: Judge the model in two steps: first the five predictions, then MSE, RMSE and MAE. Press Run and follow the results.

blocks.caption: computing predictions and metrics
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1],
              [3, 12, 2],
              [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3],
              [9, 30, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4], dtype=float)
b0, b1, b2, b3 = 20.0, -1.0, -0.5, -2.0

# 1) predictions
y_hat = b0 + b1*X[:, 0] + b2*X[:, 1] + b3*X[:, 2]
print('predictions:', y_hat)

# 2) metrics
mse_value  = np.mean((y - y_hat)**2)
rmse_value = np.sqrt(mse_value)
mae_value  = np.mean(np.abs(y - y_hat))
print('MSE :', round(mse_value, 2))
print('RMSE:', round(rmse_value, 2))
print('MAE :', round(mae_value, 2))

# 3) explained variance
r2_value = 1 - np.sum((y - y_hat)**2) / np.sum((y - y.mean())**2)
print('R2  :', round(r2_value, 2), '(negative = worse than the mean!)')

blocks.html: Read the result: MAE = 6.9 (€ 6,900), RMSE higher (7.79) — the five errors are unevenly distributed. And R² = −1.53: this model performs worse than simply predicting the mean.
The three measures from scratch with NumPy — scikit-learn ships mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error and r2_score, but seeing inside them is the point.

blocks.caption: implementing MSE, RMSE and MAE

blocks.html: The headline regression measure: R², the explained variance — what fraction of the target's variance is explained by the features.

blocks.label: explained variance
blocks.caption: The denominator measures the spread around the mean; the numerator the spread around your predictions.

rows: the model fits every data point perfectly
no better than simply predicting the mean

blocks.html: Toward 1: much variance explained. Toward 0: the line explains little. Negative is possible too — then your model is worse than always predicting the mean.

blocks.caption: implementing and applying R²
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def r2_score(y_true, y_pred):
    # numerator: spread around the predictions (model errors)
    ss_res = np.sum((y_true - y_pred)**2)
    # denominator: spread around the mean (naivest prediction)
    ss_tot = np.sum((y_true - y_true.mean())**2)
    return 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

# example values
y_true = np.array([3.0, -0.5, 2.0, 7.0])
y_pred = np.array([2.5,  0.0, 2.0, 8.0])

print('r2_score:', r2_score(y_true, y_pred))  # 0.9486081370449679

blocks.html: Compare this with the R² outcome of the car-price example: negative (−1.53). Same metric, two different worlds: here 95% of the variance is explained, there the model performs worse than the mean.

sections.title: Computing the best-fit line analytically: b1 and b0

blocks.html: For simple linear regression \( \hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x \) exact formulas give the best values in one shot — \( b_1 \) is the slope, \( b_0 \) the y-intercept.

blocks.label: slope b1
blocks.caption: Divides 'how much x and y move together' by 'how much x spreads': the slope of the best-fit line.

blocks.label: y-intercept b0
blocks.caption: The best-fit line always passes through the centroid (x̄, ȳ) of the data — once you know b1, b0 follows automatically.

blocks.html: Read \( b_1 \) like this: the numerator counts how much x and y deviate from their means together, the denominator measures the spread of x; \( b_0 \) puts the line exactly through the center of gravity \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \). Origin: set the MSE derivatives to zero — solvable in closed form for the simple line; gradient descent approaches the same values.

blocks.caption: computing b1 and b0 with the formulas (dataset A)
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

# dataset A — the same points as the interactive plot below
x = np.array([0.5, 1.19, 1.88, 2.58, 3.27, 3.96, 4.65, 5.35,
              6.04, 6.73, 7.42, 8.12, 8.81, 9.5])
y = np.array([3.08, 3.52, 5.83, 7.21, 6.72, 8.35, 10.45, 11.44,
              12.86, 13.6, 15.88, 17.08, 17.9, 19.78])

# means
x_mean = x.mean()
y_mean = y.mean()

# b1: co-movement of x and y, divided by the spread of x
b1 = np.sum((x - x_mean) * (y - y_mean)) / np.sum((x - x_mean)**2)

# b0: y-intercept — the line passes through (x_mean, y_mean)
b0 = y_mean - b1 * x_mean

print('b1 (slope)          :', b1)
print('b0 (y-intercept)    :', b0)

# the MSE at this pair is the smallest possible
y_hat = b0 + b1 * x
print('MSE at (b0, b1)     :', round(np.mean((y - y_hat)**2), 4))
print('R2 at (b0, b1)      :',
      round(1 - np.sum((y-y_hat)**2)/np.sum((y-y_mean)**2), 4))

blocks.caption: checking against scikit-learn LinearRegression
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

x = np.array([0.5, 1.19, 1.88, 2.58, 3.27, 3.96, 4.65, 5.35,
              6.04, 6.73, 7.42, 8.12, 8.81, 9.5])
y = np.array([3.08, 3.52, 5.83, 7.21, 6.72, 8.35, 10.45, 11.44,
              12.86, 13.6, 15.88, 17.08, 17.9, 19.78])

model = LinearRegression().fit(x.reshape(-1, 1), y)

print('coef_      (b1):', model.coef_[0])
print('intercept_ (b0):', model.intercept_)
print('R2           :', round(model.score(x.reshape(-1, 1), y), 4))

blocks.html: With multiple features no short closed form exists — the computer solves a system (or approximates with gradient descent). With one feature these are the two formulas.

sections.title: Exploring: does the line fit the data?

blocks.html: Three datasets, each with sliders and live metrics: find the best line and watch MSE and R² move along. Challenge yourself: compute dataset A's \( b_1 \) and \( b_0 \) by hand first (1.86 and 1.68).

blocks.title: Dataset A — clean, linear data
blocks.subtitle: Drag b0 and b1 and watch the MSE and R² update live. Analytical optimum (formulas above): b1 = 1.86, b0 = 1.68 → MSE 0.27, R² 0.99 — the chips light up green as you get close.

blocks.title: Dataset B — with one large outlier
blocks.subtitle: One point is far off (24!). Best fit: b1 = 1.42, b0 = 5.19 → MSE 18.85. Watch the live MSE show how the squared error pulls the line towards the outlier.

blocks.title: Dataset C — curved (quadratic) data
blocks.subtitle: However you place the line: a straight line cannot fit a curve. Best straight line: b1 = 1.98, b0 = −1.83 → R² 0.82 — change the model (e.g. add x² as a feature), not just the line.

blocks.html: A = the ideal case (linear, little noise); B shows one outlier blowing up the quadratic measures; C shows the limit of the model — no straight line fits, the fix is a better model (e.g. \( x^2 \) as a feature).
